::: {.callout-note}
These are the solutions to the
[Logistic regression](../lecture-02/05-logistic-regression.qmd) exercises.
Try each exercise yourself before you look.
:::

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(medicaldata)
```

`blood`, made at the top of the Logistic regression page:

```{r}
blood <- blood_storage |>
  mutate(
    recurrence = factor(Recurrence, levels = c(0, 1), labels = c("no", "yes")),
    rbc_age_group = factor(RBC.Age.Group, levels = 1:3,
                           labels = c("younger", "middle", "older"))
  )
```

## Exercise 1: Fit a logistic regression

```{r}
ggplot(blood, aes(x = rbc_age_group, fill = recurrence)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(x = "Storage age of transfused blood", y = "Proportion",
       fill = "Recurrence")
```

**(1)** About 16–18% of men had a recurrence in every group.

```{r}
rec_fit <- logistic_reg() |>
  fit(recurrence ~ rbc_age_group, data = blood)

rec_tidy <- tidy(rec_fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
rec_tidy
```

**(4)** Compared with `younger` blood,
the odds of recurrence are
`r round(rec_tidy$estimate[2], 2)` times as high with `middle` blood
(95% CI `r round(rec_tidy$conf.low[2], 2)` to `r round(rec_tidy$conf.high[2], 2)`)
and `r round(rec_tidy$estimate[3], 2)` times as high with `older` blood
(95% CI `r round(rec_tidy$conf.low[3], 2)` to `r round(rec_tidy$conf.high[3], 2)`).
Both intervals include 1,
so we have no evidence that older stored blood is associated with recurrence.
